Let \(O\) be the center of the circumcircle. Since the radius is \(1\), we have

\[
OA=OB=OC=1.
\]

We will show that \(AH\) is actually constant for every triangle satisfying the given condition.

Place the origin at \(O\), and let the position vectors of \(A,B,C\) be \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf c\). Then

\[
|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf b|=|\mathbf c|=1.
\]

For any triangle inscribed in a circle centered at the origin, the orthocenter has position vector

\[
\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c.
\]

Indeed,

\[
\mathbf h-\mathbf a=\mathbf b+\mathbf c,
\]

and

\[
(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)\cdot(\mathbf b-\mathbf c)
=|\mathbf b|^2-|\mathbf c|^2
=1-1=0,
\]

so \(AH\perp BC\). Similarly, \(BH\perp AC\). Thus \(H\) is the intersection of the altitudes.

Now,

\[
AH=|\mathbf h-\mathbf a|=|\mathbf b+\mathbf c|.
\]

Because \(\angle BAC=60^\circ\), the central angle subtending chord \(BC\) is

\[
\angle BOC=2\angle BAC=120^\circ.
\]

Therefore

\[
\mathbf b\cdot \mathbf c
=|\mathbf b||\mathbf c|\cos 120^\circ
=1\cdot 1\cdot \left(-\frac12\right)
=-\frac12.
\]

Hence

\[
AH^2=|\mathbf b+\mathbf c|^2
=|\mathbf b|^2+|\mathbf c|^2+2\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c
=1+1+2\left(-\frac12\right)
=1.
\]

So

\[
AH=1
\]

for every admissible triangle. Therefore the smallest possible value of \(AH\) is

\[
\boxed{1}.
\]
